screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, study-design, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of Training & Performance queue positions 1-12.

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: Relationship between Pre-Training     Subjective Wellness Measures, Player Load and Rating of Perceived   Exertion   Training Load in American College Football.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: In 58 Division I collegiate football players monitored across the final eight in-season weeks, higher pre-training wellness Z score and energy were trivially associated with higher player load, while lower soreness was trivially associated with lower session-RPE load.
records.limitations: This retrospective, single-team observational analysis used a custom wellness questionnaire with unestablished measurement properties; indoor sessions lacked GPS data, and only mid- to late-season observations were analyzed.
records.synthesisCaution: Use subjective wellness alongside external and internal load to inform conversation and individualization, not as a stand-alone readiness or prescription rule.

records.sourceFile: Severe exercise associated              hyponatremia in a collegiate American footbal player.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: A healthy 21-year-old Division III football defensive back developed headache, vomiting, cramping, and serum sodium of 124 mmol/L after consuming roughly 10 L before the game and additional hypotonic fluid during play; symptoms resolved and sodium normalized after follow-up.
records.limitations: This is one retrospective case without a comparator, and its individual fluid behavior, climate, clinical course, and management cannot estimate frequency or establish a general hydration prescription.
records.synthesisCaution: Treat nausea, vomiting, headache, or altered status during exertion as a medical evaluation problem; do not infer dehydration or prescribe fluids without sodium-aware clinical assessment.

records.sourceFile: The effect of tissue flossing on ankle range of motion, jump, and sprint performance in elite rugby union athletes.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Fourteen professional male rugby-union athletes completed counterbalanced flossing and control trials. Two minutes of bilateral ankle flossing produced no significant treatment-by-time effects for lunge range, countermovement jump, or 20-m sprint; small effect-size differences were observed at selected post-treatment times.
records.limitations: The crossover sample was small, only male rugby athletes were studied, effects were assessed for 30 minutes, and the comparison cannot establish injury-prevention or long-term training value.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not use ankle flossing as a proven performance or injury-prevention intervention; if used, keep it optional and judge it against athlete response and established warm-up and loading practices.

records.sourceFile: The influence of injury history on countermovement jump performance and movement strategy in professional soccer players - Implications for profiling and rehabilitation foci.pdf
records.degradedReason: The local PDF exists but pdftotext could not open it and produced no readable full text, so source-grounded eligibility, identifier, methods, results, and synthesis cannot be verified.

records.sourceFile: The influence of weekly sprint volume and maximal velocity exposures on eccentric hamstring strength in professional soccer players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: In 58 professional male footballers observed over 1.5 seasons, weekly sprint distance and efforts above 90% of maximum velocity had small inverse associations with percentage change in eccentric hamstring strength; seven to eight efforts above 90% differed from lower exposure categories, whereas efforts above 95% were not associated.
records.limitations: The observational design cannot show sprint exposure caused strength change; exposure thresholds were sparse at the highest velocity, GPS accuracy declines at maximal velocity, and injury outcomes were not directly tested.
records.synthesisCaution: Use weekly high-speed exposure and eccentric-strength monitoring as context-specific surveillance, not as a universal threshold or direct injury-risk rule.

records.sourceFile: The loading impact of training and match-play on non-contact muscle injuries in elite male soccer players - A seasonal analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: A retrospective single-season analysis of 30 English Premier League outfield players included 12 non-contact muscle injuries. In its logistic model, higher seven-day high-speed-running and sprint-distance volume were protective, whereas acute peak speed and 28-day total distance were associated with increased injury risk.
records.limitations: Only one team, one season, starting players, and 12 analyzed injuries were included. Synthetic oversampling may overfit, important internal, gym, recovery, and injury-history factors were absent, and results are associative.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not operationalize the model as an injury prediction tool; monitor exposure trends with athlete history, readiness, and clinical context and validate locally before changing load.

records.sourceFile: Quantifying demands on the hamstrings during high-speed running - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Ninety-six studies were included. As running speed rose, hamstring activation and kinetic demand increased; pooled lateral-hamstring activation during fast running was 108.1% of maximal voluntary isometric contraction, and swing-phase peak knee-flexion moment was 2.2 Nm/kg.
records.limitations: Protocols, speed definitions, muscles, samples, and biomechanical methods varied; much evidence was from healthy adults rather than injured athletes, and laboratory demand data do not establish an injury-prevention dose.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the review to justify progressive, representative high-speed exposure, not a single force target or causal claim about any one sprint variable.

records.sourceFile: Reactive strength index and its associations with measures of physical and sports performance - A systematic review with meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Across 32 studies, rebound-jump reactive strength index had moderate associations with strength and endurance and inverse associations with acceleration, maximal speed, and change-of-direction time; associations varied by task, and small-study bias was detected for acceleration and change-of-direction analyses.
records.limitations: Samples, sports, sex, training status, rebound protocol, drop height, and limb use varied; associations are cross-sectional and do not prove that increasing RSI improves sport performance.
records.synthesisCaution: Standardize the test before trend interpretation and use RSI as one component of a performance profile, not as a universal surrogate for speed, change of direction, or readiness.

records.sourceFile: Reactive strength index as a key performance indicator in different athlete populations - A systematic review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Nineteen studies were reviewed. Moderate-to-large differences in RSI generally distinguished athlete populations, and relative strength was identified as an important factor associated with RSI performance; faster athletes also tended to show higher RSI in the included comparisons.
records.limitations: This was a narrative systematic review without quantitative pooling; comparisons used varied tests and grouping methods, and cohort comparisons cannot establish whether RSI causes individual performance differences.
records.synthesisCaution: Use RSI to describe a testing construct under a stable protocol, then investigate strength and task-specific contributors rather than ranking athletes from generic norms.

records.sourceFile: Resistance training load effects on muscle hypertrophy and strength gain - Systematic review and network meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: The network meta-analysis included 28 healthy-adult studies that trained to volitional failure. Low-, moderate-, and high-load resistance training produced similar hypertrophy, while higher-load training ranked more favorably for one-repetition-maximum strength gains.
records.limitations: The comparison is restricted to training to failure and 1-RM strength; participants were largely untrained or recreationally trained, programs and muscles varied, and findings should not be extended to isometric or isokinetic strength tests.
records.synthesisCaution: Match load to the adaptation, athlete tolerance, technique, equipment, and time constraints; do not infer that all loading schemes are interchangeable or that failure is required in sport settings.

records.sourceFile: Science or hype - Non-invasive brain stimulation and sport-specific performance - Evidence from a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Twenty-five studies contributing 64 effects, all using transcranial direct-current stimulation, yielded a small overall sport-performance effect (Hedges g=0.35) with considerable heterogeneity. Effects were larger in open-skill sports and when motor executive regions were targeted, but the evidence quality was low.
records.limitations: The evidence concerns tDCS rather than all non-invasive stimulation, with heterogeneous protocols and outcomes, low quality, and limited certainty; the pooled estimate does not establish durable or safe real-world benefit.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not adopt non-invasive brain stimulation as a performance intervention on this evidence; any research use requires medical, ethical, regulatory, and safety oversight.

records.sourceFile: Sleep interventions for performance, mood and sleep outcomes in athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Twenty-seven athlete studies (617 athletes) were reviewed and 12 controlled trials entered meta-analysis. Sleep interventions improved subjective sleep quality, reduced sleepiness and negative affect, but did not improve subjective duration, objective sleep measures, or aerobic and anaerobic performance indices.
records.limitations: Studies were small and non-representative, intervention and outcome methods differed, reporting and methodological concerns were common, and objective performance evidence was limited.
records.synthesisCaution: Prioritize individualized behavioral and environmental sleep support and measure the relevant outcome; do not promise performance improvement or generalize subjective improvements to objective recovery.
